name: Uzebox
description: An open-source retro-style game console designed by Alec Bourque, built from just two main chips: an AVR microcontroller and an RGB-to-NTSC encoder. The microcontroller generates video and sound entirely in software, and a community has written dozens of homebrew games for it.
curiosities: There is no video or sound chip: the microcontroller generates the TV signal cycle-by-cycle in software.
The ATmega644 is rated for 20 MHz but runs at about 28.6 MHz, eight times the NTSC colour-burst frequency.
SparkFun sold a kit version called the Uzebox AVCore.
Its hardware schematics and software kernel are published as open source.
story: Alec Bourque designed the Uzebox in 2008 as an open-source retro console built from a single ATmega microcontroller doing all the video and sound in software.
Anyone can build one from a kit; its community has written games, emulators and demos for it, from Tetris clones to platformers.
It shows how far a tiny chip can go, and its games now run in emulation alongside the consoles that inspired it.
